title: TimeSeed: Sparse Time Series Forecasting via Context Reconstruction
one_liner: When you have external factors but almost no historical data, reconstruct what the past probably looked like, then forecast normally.
lead: Predicting the future of a measurement (like electricity demand or stock price) normally needs lots of historical records of that measurement. But in the real world you often have strong external clues (weather, calendar, events) while historical records are sparse or missing. TimeSeed solves this by first reconstructing what the missing history probably was, using the stable external factors as anchors, then forecasting forward from that reconstructed past.

problem.h2: Why sparse historical data breaks forecasting
paras: Forecasting works by finding patterns in the past. A model trained on 5 years of daily electricity records learns what Tuesday in January typically looks like, what summer demand patterns are, how weather moves demand. Then it can guess tomorrow's demand.

You have only 3 months of demand records. A naive attempt: train directly on those 3 months, use yesterday to predict tomorrow. The model sees only one summer, one winter, no Monday-Tuesday patterns that repeat yearly. It guesses badly. External signals (temperature, day-of-week, holidays) are available and stable, but the model cannot anchor them to the sparse history because there is too little past to build the map.

callout.html: Sparse historical records starve the model of patterns, so it cannot learn how external factors drive the measurement.

paras: Most forecasters take the measurement values directly: yesterday's 450 kilowatts, today's 470 kilowatts. TimeSeed instead takes a different input: it uses external signals to rebuild the historical context where records are missing, creating a synthetic past.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: reconstructed history alignment
hidden.name: How well external signals predict missing values
paras: The hidden quantity is how strongly external factors (weather, calendar, events) predict the measurement when historical records are sparse. TimeSeed measures this by training a small linear model on just the external signals and the few real measurement records available, then checking: can the external signals alone generate plausible guesses for the missing weeks? If yes, the external signals are reliable anchors and reconstruction will work. If no, external signals are weak and the reconstruction will be noisy.
The paper exploits this by assuming external signals are stable (they happen on schedule and have regular effects), so their predictive signal is trustworthy even when historical records are few.

heat.caption: Darker cells are stronger signals. Marked cells use external factors reliably.

reads.html: When external factors (weather, day-of-week) are stable and predictive, you can use them to guess what missing historical records probably were, then learn the pattern from that guessed history.

TimeSeed jointly exploits the stability of external sequences and sparse historical observations to reconstruct accurate historical representations, measured as how well external signals predict the few recorded values.

mechanism.h2: Why reconstructing the past makes forecasting work
paras: Forecasting learns patterns from repetition: "Mondays are usually 10% higher," "summer peaks at 3pm." With only 3 months of data, the model never sees a Monday in January, or two full summers, so it cannot learn these repeating patterns. Reconstruction solves this: use the external signals (which cover months of stable context) to predict what the full history probably looked like. Now the model can see multiple Mondays, multiple seasons, the actual patterns.

The mechanism works because external signals are stable: weather follows seasonal rules, day-of-week is deterministic, holidays are known. A tiny linear model trained on just the few real records can learn to trust these signals ("when it is cold, demand probably rises"). Once learned, that same signal-to-value mapping fills in the missing months. The result is a synthetic history that is plausible (it respects what external factors should do) and complete (no gaps). Train a second model on this complete history, and it learns the real patterns.

stages.s: Sparse measurements and full external signals
Small linear model learns external-to-measurement mapping
Fill missing history using learned mapping
Train second linear model on complete reconstructed history

math.words: predicted_value = weight_1 times external_signal_1 plus weight_2 times external_signal_2 plus ... plus bias
math.equation: y_reconstructed = w_1 * x_1 + w_2 * x_2 + ... + w_k * x_k + b

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Say we have three external signals: temperature (in Celsius), day-of-week (1-7), holiday-flag (0 or 1).
After training on real records, the model learned: w_temp=2.0, w_day=5.0, w_holiday=-10.0, b=100.
Missing Wednesday in January, temp 5C, no holiday: y = 2.0*5 + 5.0*3 + (-10.0)*0 + 100 = 10 + 15 + 0 + 100 = 125.
The holiday flag cuts 10 units (learned from real holiday records), showing the model picked up the pattern.

math.note: The weights are learned from whichever real measurement records exist, then applied to fill all time points (real and missing alike) for the full history.

items.b: External signals are weak or non-predictive.
items.html: If external factors (temperature, holidays, day-of-week) do not actually drive the measurement, reconstruction produces noise instead of plausible history. The problem: you cannot know this until you try. Solution: validate that external signals predict real records well before using them to reconstruct.

items.b: The sparse records you do have are outliers or mislabeled.
items.html: If the few measurements available are corrupted or exceptional, the model learns the wrong signal-to-value mapping, then fills all missing time points incorrectly. Solution: clean real records carefully before training the reconstruction model.

items.b: External signals change their behavior over time.
items.html: If the relationship between weather and demand shifts (e.g., new building insulation, different occupancy patterns), the early sparse records taught one pattern, but reconstruction applies it to later months when the pattern is different. Solution: use only recent external signals and sparse records from the same era.

items.b: Done right: validate and align eras.
items.html: Check that external signals predict available records well (correlation above a threshold). Ensure sparse records and external signals are from the same time period and context. Train the reconstruction model separately for different seasons if behavior changes.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy forecasting task: you have daily measurements for January and March, but February is missing. You have daily temperature, day-of-week, and a holiday flag for all three months. Split January into a training set (first week) and validation set (rest of January). Train a linear model from first week's measurements and external signals. Use this model to fill February. Append reconstructed February to real March. Now train a forecaster on Jan+reconstructed-Feb, then test on March.
demo.closing: The demo must show: the naive method (train only on January) makes larger forecast errors on March than TimeSeed (trained on January plus reconstructed February). This proves that filling the gap with a signal-based guess gives the model more patterns to learn from.
